The shoe decomposition · short report

How much of the post-2017 marathon speed-up is the shoe?

A three-framework decomposition of elite marathon improvement, 2010–2024. Jeremy Lee, May 2026.

Nike’s Vaporfly 4% went on general sale in 2017, and elite marathon times dropped quickly after it. This report asks how many seconds of that drop the shoe accounts for, using 1,908 elite performances and three methods that control for different things.

Pooled shoe contribution
67 seconds
95% CI 36–99 s · about 0.9% of a 2:05 marathon

The question

Of the elite marathon improvement between the pre-Vaporfly era (2010–2016) and the post-Vaporfly era (2018–2024), how much, in seconds, comes from the shoe? 2017 is a transition year and sits in neither window.

No single method answers that cleanly, so the analysis runs three and compares them.

Framework 1: difference-in-differences

Road marathon improvement minus track 10,000 m improvement over the same window, with the track change rescaled to marathon time. Track racing did not take up carbon plates at the same rate, so anything that sped up both events cancels out.

Framework 2: within-athlete paired

Athletes with at least two elite marathons in each era. Comparing a runner with themselves holds genetics and training history fixed. The race tables carry no ages, so the change is not age-adjusted.

Framework 3: cohort survival

Counts of sub-2:10 (men) and sub-2:25 (women) performances per year, a changepoint search on those counts, and the shift in the top-30 median between eras, of which 55% is attributed to shoes.

The three estimates

Framework 1. Difference-in-differences (road vs track, women-only pre-era)
111 s
[131, 253]
Framework 2. Within-athlete paired (n=17, p=0.26)
47 s
[-25, 137]
Framework 3. Cohort survival (changepoint 2020)
58 s
[46, 111]
Pooled (weighted by inverse squared CI width)
67 s
[36, 99]

The difference-in-differences interval lies above its point estimate because the point uses year medians and the bootstrap resamples row means. Both are reported as computed.

Sub-2:10 became more common, but not five times more

The pre-era averaged 23 sub-2:10 men’s performances per year across the major-marathon dataset and the post-era averaged 29, a 1.25× rise (1.39× for women under 2:25). Running media often quotes three to five times. That figure covers a wider set of races, including second-tier marathons, where the middle of the field has more room to move.

Track 10,000 m improved far less

Track times did improve: Cheptegei ran 26:11 in 2020 and Chebet 28:54 in 2024. Across the eras the women’s track numbers moved about 0.3% while the women’s road marathon top-30 median moved about 1.6%. That gap, roughly five to one, is the main evidence for something road-specific, and the shoe is the most obvious road-specific change. The track control is thin, though: 27 performances, and only 2016 on the pre-era side.

What it adds up to

The shoe accounts for about a minute of elite marathon time, close to 1% and well short of the 4% running-economy gain measured on treadmills. Running economy is not race time, and deeper East African fields, pace-controlled races and altitude training changed over the same years. The shoe gets most of the credit in public argument partly because it has a release date.

Limits

  • The track control has 27 rows, and its pre-era side is one year of women’s results. Framework 1 is the weakest of the three for that reason.
  • The within-athlete sample is 17 runners and the paired t-test is not significant (p = 0.26).
  • The 55% shoe share in Framework 3 is a modeling choice, not an estimate.
  • Era stands in for shoe use. Nobody’s footwear is recorded per race.

Reproduce

git clone https://github.com/lyhjeremy/marathon-shoe-revolution-decomposition.git
cd marathon-shoe-revolution-decomposition
pip install -r requirements.txt
python src/analysis.py

Under a minute on an M1 MacBook. The PDF report has the sensitivity analysis and full limitations; the notebook in notebooks/ reproduces every number cell by cell.
